text_to_speech: Hi, I'm here today with Sergio Prado from Embedded Labworks. Sergio, can you tell us a little bit about Embedded Labworks? Sure. Hello guys, Embedded Labworks is a company located in  São Paulo, Brazil. We are specialized in training and consulting services on Embedded Software Development, and we have a lot of trainings and we are mainly focused on Embedded Linux, Embedded Android, and RTOS's like FreeRTOS, MQX,  and things like that. So  Sergio, we are here today for a sponsored training by Toradex. Can you tell us a little bit more about this training? Sure. We had an idea of doing a training session on Embedded Linux  programming, that's a necessity of the market here in Brazil, that people are starting to use a lot of Embedded Linux in their systems and then we decided to do a Embedded Linux programming session in a 4 series here in Brazil, and I think it was a success, that people liked it a lot. The training mainly focuses on teaching the people how to develop Embedded Linux applications in C language, so we start and learn a little bit about the environment like how can we used GCC and GDB to develop and debug applications in Linux. We learned a little bit about how to integrate the Eclipse environment using the Toradex board. We are using in this training a board from Toradex of course, it's a Colibri baseboard with a module from Toradex.  Colibri VF50 with the Viola Carrier Board.  Right, and we developed here in Brazil, an expansion board called Ipê board, with a lot of peripherals like LEDs and buzzers and displays, buttons, and things like that, so we could develop a lot of exercise in the training. And, in the training we learned how to access the LEDs in the board, the buttons, the accelerometer, buzzer, we develop a lot of applications using this interface. One of the last exercises is how to monitor the board, and identify if the board is positioned horizontally and the table show if we move the board a little bit, the buzzer will be started. Yes. And this accelerometer is over I2C, right? Yes. And the buzzer? The buzzer is on the PWM channel. OK. Nice! Cool demo. And Sergio, why is Embedded Linux such a popular  OS for embedded systems? There are a lot of reasons. One  of the main reasons of course, is because it's free software. So, we can download the source code, we can change, improve, and contribute with the community, but of course that is not the only reason, using Linux we have a lot of things that already have been done by the community, so it's a lot easier to implement an application in Linux because we have something like the TCP stack ready, USB stacks ready, Graphical stack ready, a lot of applications ready to be used. So, developing an application using Linux is much easier. There are a lot of tools ready to be used, so using Linux we don't need to buy any tools or software. You can use only open source and free software and that's a good advantage we don't have pay royalties to anyone, so I think that's the main reason to use Linux on embedded systems, and today it's standard. Yeah, I think most of the SoC providers already provide some sort of BSP for  their processors with Linux, right? OK, so, this was Sergio Prado from Embedded Labworks, our partner in Brazil. If you want to contact us, please go to toradex.com, or e-labworks.com. Thank you.

youtube_description:
Guilherme Fernandes, CEO, Toradex Brasil interviews Sergio Prado of Embedded Labworks. The highlights of the discussion include;
- The Embedded Linux training series sponsored by Toradex in partnership with Embedded labworks
- Key takeaways of the training session
- How embedded engineers are benefited by the training
- Why embedded Linux is a popular OS for embedded systems
